paras: The attempted lynching of Albert Going took place at Rome, Georgia, on the night of September 18-19, 1903, when crowds gathered at the Floyd County jail threatening to take Going, a Black man charged with attempted criminal assault on a white girl. The sheriff refused to give him up, Governor Terrell sent militia to guard the jail, and Going was moved to Atlanta, later tried under military guard and sentenced to twenty years. The case drew notice as an instance of a Southern governor and sheriff turning back a mob, and some reports noted doubt about the charge itself.

On the morning of September 17 Going was arrested and jailed at Rome on a charge of attempted criminal assault on the daughter of T. B. Peyton, a planter living near the town. According to the Savannah Morning News, Going asked the girl, who was picking cotton, whether she wanted candy; she screamed, and her mother drove him off with a shotgun. Other versions said he seized her, and two reported that the mother's shot wounded him before a posse under Deputy Sheriff Broach captured him.

The Savannah report said the girl was weak-minded from injuries in a runaway accident, could not remember what took place, and gave a 'hysterical and incoherent' account. By evening rumors of lynching ran through Rome, and Sheriff Donahoo let it be known that Going could be taken only over his dead body.

On the evening of September 18 men and boys gathered near the jail and courthouse, about three hundred by ten o'clock according to the New York Sun. Threats to take the prisoner were heard on all sides, and the sheriff was told that a thousand men gathering in the countryside had threatened to kill any deputy who resisted. The sheriff wired Governor Terrell, who ordered Major R. L. Williamson to mobilize what troops he could.

Williamson brought about thirty men of the Hill City Cadets to the jail amid hoots and some cheers, and the Savannah Morning News reported that the four or five hundred men there then dispersed. The Sun gave a different close: at about 2 a.m. on September 19 the mob moved on the jail and demanded the prisoner, and the sheriff, declaring that no lynching party would get Going while he lived, told it there was doubt of his guilt and talked it into dispersing.
Later on September 19 Going was taken to Atlanta and lodged in the tower, on the order of Judge Henry according to the Associated Press or of the governor according to the Sun.

On October 14 Going was brought back to Rome under guard of militia companies and tried in the Superior Court with every entrance to the courthouse guarded. The girl, then given as eighteen, testified that he had threatened to kill her if she did not submit. The jury found him guilty with a recommendation to mercy, and Judge Henry sentenced him to twenty years in the penitentiary. No arrest of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage.

Coverage came almost entirely from the white press: Rome specials in the Savannah Morning News and an Associated Press dispatch that ran nearly verbatim from Richmond to Bemidji, Minnesota. Southern headlines named Going a 'Negro Rapist', a 'Black Brute' and a 'Negro Fiend' before any trial, even as the Savannah report conceded that the girl could not remember what happened.

The New York Sun, under 'Georgia Troops Foil Mob', reported the sheriff's doubts about the charge. The Arizona Republican's editorial observed that there was doubt of guilt 'but the mob sought to kill him, just the same', and saw a growing Southern respect for the courts. The only Black-press report found was a syndicated brief in the Baltimore Afro-American on September 26, headlined 'The High Wanted Him' (the Bridgeton, New Jersey, Pioneer ran the same text as 'The Mob Wanted Him'), reporting the threats and the move to Atlanta without comment.

The accuser's name appears as Lessie, Lizzie and Leslie Peyton and her age as fifteen, sixteen and eighteen. Whether the crowd broke up when the troops arrived, as the Savannah correspondent wrote, or after rushing the jail at 2 a.m., as the Sun reported, is not settled by the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Going
bases: A crowd gathered at the Floyd County jail threatening to take Going, a Black prisoner charged with attempted assault, and by one account moved on the jail and demanded him before the sheriff and militia turned it away (A4, A5, A11, A21).

Going was not killed: troops guarded the jail, the crowd dispersed, and he was moved to Atlanta, tried and sentenced to twenty years (A5, A11, A12, A22). The episode is an attempted lynching by a crowd of hundreds acting on a rape-related accusation (A5, A11, A21).

A Rome special in the Savannah Morning News, the Associated Press dispatch and a separate Rome report in the New York Sun agree that a crowd gathered at the jail with threats to take Going and that militia were ordered out (A4, A5, A11).

accounts.label: Rome specials of Sept. 17
accounts.gist: Going was arrested by a posse after a mother drove him away from her daughter with a shotgun; versions differ on whether he seized the girl or only spoke to her and whether he was wounded; two said the posse was orderly and no lynching was attempted.

accounts.label: Associated Press, Atlanta, Sept. 18
accounts.gist: A mob gathered at the jail with threats to take Going; the sheriff heard a thousand men were gathering who threatened to kill deputies, and the governor ordered militia out.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News Rome special, Sept. 18
accounts.gist: Thirty militiamen reached the jail, where four or five hundred men dispersed on their arrival amid hoots and cheers.

accounts.label: New York Sun, Rome, Sept. 19
accounts.gist: A crowd of about 300 planned to storm the jail; at 2 a.m. the mob moved on it and demanded Going, and the sheriff dispersed it after saying there was doubt of his guilt.

accounts.label: Black press (syndicated brief)
accounts.gist: Going was moved to Atlanta after many threats of lynching and the calling out of the militia.

framing.detail: Georgia and Alabama papers headlined Going as a 'Negro Rapist' and 'Black Brute' before trial, while the Savannah report itself said the girl 'cannot remember what took place' and the Sun quoted the sheriff on doubt of guilt.
The AP Atlanta dispatch ran nearly verbatim from Richmond to Minnesota under headlines such as 'LYNCHING THREATENED DOWN IN GEORGIA' and 'Militia Guard Negro Fiend'.
The Arizona Republican's editorial 'Mob Law Prevented' praised the governor and sheriff and argued that no state can be governed by mob law.
The Baltimore Afro-American ran the syndicated brief, its headline garbled to 'The High Wanted Him', without comment.
